quote: War is a matter of life and death, and must be studied carefully.
Consider moral influence, weather, terrain, leadership, and discipline.
Compare the opposing sides before predicting success.
All warfare is based on deception.
When capable, appear incapable.
When active, appear inactive.
When near, make the opponent believe you are far away.
When far away, make the opponent believe you are near.
Offer an advantage to draw the opponent forward.
If the opponent is secure everywhere, prepare carefully.
If the opponent is stronger, avoid direct confrontation.
Attack where the opponent is unprepared.
Appear where you are not expected.
Keep the plans that lead to victory secret.
Careful calculation before conflict increases the chance of success.
A prolonged campaign drains strength and resources.
When victory takes too long, enthusiasm fades.
There is no example of a nation benefiting from prolonged warfare.
Understand the dangers of conflict before expecting to profit from it.
Value victory, not prolonged struggle.
Preserving something intact is better than destroying it.
Winning every battle is not the highest form of excellence.
The highest excellence is overcoming resistance without fighting.
The highest form of strategy is to frustrate the opponent's plans.
Next best is preventing opposing forces from joining together.
Attacking fortified positions should be a last resort.
A skillful leader overcomes forces without unnecessary conflict.
If you greatly outnumber the opponent, surround them.
If evenly matched, you may offer battle.
If weaker, know when withdrawal is necessary.
Know when to engage and when not to engage.
Know how to handle both superior and inferior forces.
Preparation creates opportunities for victory.
Know the opponent and know yourself.
Knowing yourself and your opponent removes much uncertainty.
Knowing yourself but not the opponent brings mixed results.
Knowing neither yourself nor the opponent invites failure.
First make yourself difficult to defeat.
Then wait for an opportunity to overcome the opponent.
Preventing your own defeat lies within your control.
An opportunity for victory often comes from the opponent.
One may understand victory without yet being able to achieve it.
Skillful defense makes defeat difficult.
Great skill is not merely seeing an obvious victory.
The clever strategist wins with apparent ease.
Reliable success comes from avoiding mistakes.
Put yourself where defeat is unlikely, then recognize the right moment.
The victorious strategist prepares success before seeking confrontation.
Managing many people follows the same principles as managing a few.
Organization makes a large force manageable.
Direct methods begin contests; indirect methods often decide them.
Direct and indirect methods can produce endless combinations.
Few basic elements can create countless combinations.
Apparent disorder can conceal discipline.
Apparent weakness can conceal strength.
Use circumstances to create momentum.
A skilled strategist seeks victory from the situation, not from individuals alone.
The one who arrives first is rested; the one who rushes in later is exhausted.
Make the opponent respond to you rather than responding to them.
Advantages can entice an opponent to move.
Appear where the opponent must hurry to defend.
Move rapidly toward places where you are unexpected.
Progress is easiest where there is little opposition.
Success is more certain when you target what is poorly defended.
Defend positions that are difficult to challenge.
The skilled attacker leaves the opponent uncertain where to defend.
The skilled defender leaves the opponent uncertain where to attack.
Force the opponent to reveal their formation while concealing your own.
Concentrate your strength while encouraging the opponent to divide theirs.
Numbers alone do not guarantee advantage.
Do not repeat tactics simply because they succeeded once.
Adapt your methods to changing circumstances.
Military tactics resemble water.
Water avoids heights and moves toward lower ground.
Likewise, avoid strength and move toward weakness.
As water shapes itself to terrain, strategy must shape itself to circumstances.
There are no permanent conditions and no permanently successful method.
Turning a difficult route into an advantage is part of maneuvering.
An organized force can maneuver; an undisciplined crowd cannot.
Do not take the bait an opponent deliberately offers.
Do not interfere with a force returning home without considering its motivation.
Leave an apparent escape route rather than creating needless desperation.
Do not press a desperate opponent without thought.
Some roads should not be followed.
Some forces should not be challenged.
Some positions are not worth contesting.
A leader must understand how circumstances change the correct strategy.
In favorable conditions, consider what could go wrong.
In difficult conditions, look for what can be gained.
Observe carefully; small signs can reveal larger intentions.
Movement among trees can reveal an approaching force.
Dust and movement can reveal what is happening at a distance.
Order and discipline strengthen confidence.
Understand terrain and use it appropriately.
Know the terrain, the conditions, yourself, and the opposition.
Different situations require different responses.
Speed is essential when exploiting an opportunity.
Move only when there is an advantage to be gained.
Do not act merely from anger; circumstances and emotions change.
Knowledge of the opponent's situation should come from reliable intelligence.
